demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette: Elias, seventy-eight and of Syrian descent, sits in the armchair, his shoulders tight, eyes fixed on the floorboards as if counting the gaps between the planks. He traces the rim of his teacup with a thumb worn smooth by decades of fieldwork. Twelve years ago, the shoring gives way without warning. Dirt and steel collapse into a sudden, violent rush. He remembers the sound first-a wet, heavy thud that stops his breath. Then the silence. Amir lies pinned beneath the collapsed trench wall, his legs twisted at an impossible angle. Elias throws himself forward, digging with bare hands until his knuckles split, but the weight never shifts. Paramedics arrive too late for the spine. Amir walks with a cane now, and Elias has never looked him in the eye since. In the months that follow, the certainty Elias built his career on begins to fracture. He has spent forty years translating the earth's behavior into models and safety protocols, yet he cannot model the gravity that betrays him. The intrusions arrive without warning. He wakes at 3 a.m., the smell of damp earth and iron thick in his throat, his chest heaving as if the soil were filling his lungs again. He stops sleeping on his back. He tells his wife, Nadia, that he prefers it, but he really cannot bear to feel pinned. He avoids anything that resembles a construction site. When his grandson's school announces a foundation pour, Elias cancels their Saturday outing, claiming a migraine. He sits in the garden instead, watching the sprinklers hiss, flinching at the sharp crack of a distant jackhammer. His hands, usually steady enough to pipette microliters of mercury, tremble when he picks up a trowel. He tells me he feels like a traitor to his own expertise, that his scientific training has become a cage rather than a compass. Now, Elias works only in climate modeling from a quiet home office. He tells colleagues he is semi-retired, but the truth is simpler: he cannot stand the sight of disturbed ground. Nadia notes how he has grown distant, how he once animated every sunset with geological stories and now answers in monosyllables. When he speaks in session, his voice drops to a careful murmur. He describes the weight of his guilt not as a single heavy stone, but as a slow accumulation, layer upon layer, pressing down until he feels he is suffocating under the sheer weight of his own error. He believes he has become unreliable, a contaminant in his own life. He flinches when Nadia reaches for his shoulder. He checks the gas stove four times before leaving. He pours the tea with the unhurried rhythm his father taught him, a small anchor in a life that feels untethered. He keeps a notebook of dates, marking each year since the trench, as if tallying time could somehow balance a scale that refuses to level. He speaks of the field site in a flat, rehearsed tone, yet his pupils dilate and his breathing shallows when the wind shifts, carrying the damp, mineral scent of late autumn rain. Nadia sits beside him, her hand resting lightly on his forearm, a quiet testament to a marriage that has weathered decades of discovery and years of this slow unraveling.
